question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
answer:
You end up controlling exactly one of your opponent's turns (their very next turn), you do get a second Emrakul, the Promised End (as a token), but copying the Emrakul, the Promised End spell itself does NOT create a second control-a-turn trigger.

Here's the play-by-play (assuming a two-player game, since you refer to "my opponent" singular — in a multiplayer game the copied trigger could instead target a different opponent, which would change the outcome; see note below):

1) You cast Emrakul, the Promised End. Its triggered ability ("When you cast this spell, you gain control of target opponent during that player's next turn. After that turn, that player takes an extra turn.") goes on the stack targeting your opponent.

2) You activate Lithoform Engine's first ability ({2},{T}: Copy target activated or triggered ability you control) targeting that trigger. This ability resolves first (it's on top of the stack), putting a copy of the Emrakul trigger onto the stack above the original — copying its target too, since you have no other legal opponent to redirect it to (Lithoform Engine ruling #3; rule 707.10, 707.10b).

3) Now two instances of the "gain control / extra turn" trigger are on the stack, both targeting the same opponent. The copy resolves first, creating a control effect over that opponent's next turn plus a delayed triggered ability ("after that turn, that player takes an extra turn") — this delayed trigger is created per rule 603.7h. Then the original trigger resolves, creating a second control effect over the *same* upcoming turn, plus its own separate delayed extra-turn trigger.

4) Per Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14, multiple player-controlling effects that affect the same player overwrite each other — only the last one created actually governs that turn. Since both effects are aimed at the same single "next turn" of your opponent, you only ever control that one turn, not two. However, the ruling also states that each ability's effect still creates its own extra turn. So after that controlled turn ends, both delayed triggers fire, and per rule 500.7 two separate extra turns are added for your opponent, one at a time (the most recently created extra turn is taken first). Those two extra turns belong to your opponent — you don't control them (nothing here gives you control of them).

5) Separately, you untap Lithoform Engine with Voltaic Key and use its third ability ({4},{T}: Copy target permanent spell you control) on the Emrakul, the Promised End spell itself. When that copy resolves, rule 111.13 turns it into a token with all of Emrakul, the Promised End's characteristics (13/13, flying, trample, protection from instants, and its cost-reduction/cast-trigger text) — so yes, you get a second Emrakul, the Promised End as a token permanent.

6) That second Emrakul does NOT retrigger the "when you cast this spell" ability. A copy made by Lithoform Engine is never cast — rule 707.10 and 707.10b both state a copy of a spell isn't cast, and Lithoform Engine ruling #6 explicitly confirms creating the copy won't cause cast-triggered abilities to trigger. Since Emrakul, the Promised End's control effect only triggers "when you cast this spell," the copied permanent spell gives you no additional control-a-turn trigger.

Net result: you control 1 of your opponent's turns, your opponent ends up owing 2 extra turns afterward (not controlled by you), and you have two Emrakul, the Promised Ends on the battlefield (one original, one token) but only one control trigger ever fired twice (not two separate cast triggers).

Assumption note: I assumed a two-player game so both triggered-ability instances had to target the same (only) opponent. In a multiplayer game, when copying the trigger with Lithoform Engine you could choose a different opponent as the new target, in which case you'd control one turn from each of two different opponents instead of stacking two effects on the same player's turn.

cited_text.500.7: Some effects can give a player extra turns. They do this by adding the turns directly after the specified turn. If a player is given multiple extra turns, the extra turns are added one at a time. If multiple players are given extra turns, the extra turns are added one at a time, in APNAP order (see rule 101.4). The most recently created turn will be taken first.
cited_text.603.7h: An effect may create a delayed triggered ability that can do something at a later time. A delayed triggered ability will contain “when,” “whenever,” or “at,” although that word won’t usually begin the ability. An activated or triggered ability may create a delayed triggered ability that triggers when the ability that created it has resolved a certain number of times in a turn. In that case, that delayed triggered ability is created only once, during the appropriate resolution of that ability.
cited_text.111.13: A copy of a permanent spell becomes a token as it resolves. The token has the characteristics of the spell that became that token. The token is not “created” for the purposes of any replacement effects or triggered abilities that refer to creating a token.

A copy of a spell or ability copies both the characteristics of the spell or ability and all decisions made for it, including modes, targets, the value of X, and additional or alternative costs. If an effect of the copy refers to objects used to pay its costs, it uses the objects used to pay the costs of the original spell or ability. A copy of a spell is owned by the player under whose control it was put on the stack. A copy of a spell or ability is controlled by the player under whose control it was put on the stack. A copy of a spell is itself a spell, even though it has no spell card associated with it. A copy of an ability is itself an ability. A player casts Fork, targeting an Emerald Charm. Fork reads, “Copy target instant or sorcery spell, except that the copy is red. You may choose new targets for the copy.” Emerald Charm is a modal green instant. When the Fork resolves, it puts a copy of the Emerald Charm on the stack except the copy is red, not green. The copy has the same mode that was chosen for the original Emerald Charm. It does not necessarily have the same target, but only because Fork allows choosing of new targets. Fling is an instant that reads, “As an additional cost to cast this spell, sacrifice a creature” and “Fling deals damage equal to the sacrificed creature’s power to any target.” When determining how much damage a copy of Fling deals, it checks the power of the creature sacrificed to pay for the original Fling. Dawnglow Infusion is a sorcery that reads, “You gain X life if {G} was spent to cast this spell and X life if {W} was spent to cast it.” Because mana isn’t an object, a copy of Dawnglow Infusion won’t cause you to gain any life, no matter what mana was spent to cast the original spell.

If the ability refers to its source by name, the copy refers to that same object and not to any other object with the same name. question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
answer:
With X=0, Awaken the Woods costs {1}{G}{G} (3 total mana: 1 generic + 2 green) — but you get zero Forest Dryad tokens, since X is locked in at 0 when you announce the spell. You should instead choose X=2, which also ends up costing {1}{G}{G} (3 total mana) but gets you 2 Forest Dryad tokens — the best value point given this cost math.

Here's the breakdown, following the order given for interactions like this: start from the announced cost, apply any straight cost increases, then apply cost reductions, then finally apply Trinisphere's floor (Trinisphere ruling #0).

Awaken the Woods' cost is {X}{G}{G}. When you cast it, you announce X as part of casting the spell, and that value is locked in for the spell on the stack (rule 107.3a); Trinisphere's later cost adjustment doesn't change what X actually is, and Awaken the Woods' text defines X only as the number of tokens created, not as something Trinisphere can retroactively bump (rule 202.3e confirms the spell's mana value/X value doesn't move because of how much mana you ultimately pay).

- X=0: base cost {G}{G} (2 mana, since X contributes {0}). Your green-spell reduction of {1} tries to cut the generic portion, but the generic component is already {0} and can't go below {0} (rule 601.2f), so the cost stays {G}{G} = 2 mana. Trinisphere then checks: 2 mana is less than three mana, so the cost becomes three mana total, with the extra 1 payable in any color (Trinisphere's text; Trinisphere ruling #0). Final cost: {1}{G}{G} (3 mana: 1 generic of any color + 2 green). You get X=0 tokens — nothing for 3 mana.
- X=1: base cost {1}{G}{G} (3 mana: 1 generic + 2 green). Your reduction removes {1} generic, leaving {G}{G} (2 mana). Trinisphere sees 2 < 3 and bumps it back to 3 mana total, i.e. {1}{G}{G} again. You pay the same 3 mana as the X=0 case, but now get X=1 token.
- X=2: base cost {2}{G}{G} (4 mana: 2 generic + 2 green). Your reduction removes {1} generic, leaving {1}{G}{G} (3 mana: 1 generic + 2 green). Trinisphere checks: 3 mana is not less than three mana, so it does nothing. Final cost stays {1}{G}{G} (3 mana), and you get X=2 tokens — the same 3-mana price as X=0 or X=1, but for 2 tokens instead of 0 or 1.
- X=3 and higher: the reduction still only knocks off {1} generic, so each additional point of X now costs you a full extra mana (X=3 costs {2}{G}{G}, 4 mana, for 3 tokens), just like normal. So X=2 is the unique 'break-even' point where your cost reduction exactly cancels out down to Trinisphere's three-mana floor without wasting any of it — it's the most tokens you can get without paying more than the Trinisphere-mandated minimum of 3 mana.

Assumption: your reduction effect ('green spells cost {1} less') only reduces generic mana, consistent with the standard rule that cost reductions can't touch colored symbols and can't go below {0} generic (rule 601.2f). If your actual reduction effect works differently (e.g., reduces colored mana), the numbers above would change.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

cited_text.601.2f: To cast a spell is to take it from where it is (usually the hand), put it on the stack, and pay its costs, so that it will eventually resolve and have its effect. Casting a spell includes proposal of the spell (rules 601.2a–d) and determination and payment of costs (rules 601.2f–h). To cast a spell, a player follows the steps listed below, in order. A player must be legally allowed to cast the spell to begin this process (see rule 601.3). If a player is unable to comply with the requirements of a step listed below while performing that step, the casting of the spell is illegal; the game returns to the moment before the casting of that spell was proposed (see rule 733, “Handling Illegal Actions”). The player determines the total cost of the spell. Usually this is just the mana cost. Some spells have additional or alternative costs. Some effects may increase or reduce the cost to pay, or may provide other alternative costs. Costs may include paying mana, tapping permanents, sacrificing permanents, discarding cards, and so on. The total cost is the mana cost or alternative cost (as determined in rule 601.2b), plus all additional costs and cost increases, and minus all cost reductions. If multiple cost reductions apply, the player may apply them in any order. If the mana component of the total cost is reduced to nothing by cost reduction effects, it is considered to be {0}. It can’t be reduced to less than {0}. Once the total cost is determined, any effects that directly affect the total cost are applied. Then the resulting total cost becomes “locked in.” If effects would change the total cost after this time, they have no effect.
cited_text.601.2b: To cast a spell is to take it from where it is (usually the hand), put it on the stack, and pay its costs, so that it will eventually resolve and have its effect. Casting a spell includes proposal of the spell (rules 601.2a–d) and determination and payment of costs (rules 601.2f–h). To cast a spell, a player follows the steps listed below, in order. A player must be legally allowed to cast the spell to begin this process (see rule 601.3). If a player is unable to comply with the requirements of a step listed below while performing that step, the casting of the spell is illegal; the game returns to the moment before the casting of that spell was proposed (see rule 733, “Handling Illegal Actions”). If the spell is modal, the player announces the mode choice (see rule 700.2). If the player wishes to splice any cards onto the spell (see rule 702.47), they reveal those cards in their hand. If the spell has alternative or additional costs that will be paid as it’s being cast such as buyback or kicker costs (see rules 118.8 and 118.9), the player announces their intentions to pay any or all of those costs (see rule 601.2f). A player can’t apply two alternative methods of casting or two alternative costs to a single spell. If the spell has a variable cost that will be paid as it’s being cast (such as an {X} in its mana cost; see rule 107.3), the player announces the value of that variable. If the value of that variable is defined in the text of the spell by a choice that player would make later in the announcement or resolution of the spell, that player makes that choice at this time instead of that later time. If a cost that will be paid as the spell is being cast includes hybrid mana symbols, the player announces the nonhybrid equivalent cost they intend to pay. If a cost that will be paid as the spell is being cast includes Phyrexian mana symbols, the player announces whether they intend to pay 2 life or a corresponding colored mana cost for each of those symbols. Previously made choices (such as choosing to cast a spell with flashback from a graveyard or choosing to cast a creature with morph face down) may restrict the player’s options when making these choices.
cited_text.107.3a: Many objects use the letter X as a placeholder for a number that needs to be determined. Some objects have abilities that define the value of X; the rest let their controller choose the value of X. If a spell or activated ability has a mana cost, alternative cost, additional cost, and/or activation cost with an {X}, [-X], or X in it, and the value of X isn’t defined by the text of that spell or ability, the controller of that spell or ability chooses and announces the value of X as part of casting the spell or activating the ability. (See rule 601, “Casting Spells.”) While a spell is on the stack, any X in its mana cost or in any alternative cost or additional cost it has equals the announced value. While an activated ability is on the stack, any X in its activation cost equals the announced value.
cited_text.202.3e: The mana value of an object is a number equal to the total amount of mana in its mana cost, regardless of color. When calculating the mana value of an object with an {X} in its mana cost, X is treated as 0 while the object is not on the stack, and X is treated as the number chosen for it while the object is on the stack.

question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
answer:
Yes, you can target Grist, the Hunger Tide with Animate Dead while it's in your graveyard, but the net result is that Grist enters the battlefield only briefly and is then sacrificed.

Why targeting works: per [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1], "anywhere but on the battlefield, Grist is a Legendary Planeswalker Creature — Grist Insect," so while sitting in your graveyard it is a creature card, exactly what Animate Dead's enchant ability ("enchant creature card in a graveyard") requires. Animate Dead is cast as an Aura targeting Grist, the Hunger Tide in the graveyard, and enters the battlefield attached to that card [702.128a is not directly relevant here since this is Animate Dead's own printed text, not embalm; see Animate Dead ruling #1].

What happens on resolution: Animate Dead's enters-the-battlefield triggered ability returns Grist, the Hunger Tide to the battlefield under your control and tries to attach Animate Dead to it again [Animate Dead ruling #1]. But the instant Grist, the Hunger Tide hits the battlefield, it stops being a creature — per [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1], "Once it enters the battlefield, it is no longer a creature and is just a planeswalker." Since Animate Dead can only be attached to a creature (it needs a legal creature object to enchant), it cannot legally attach to Grist, the Hunger Tide once Grist is on the battlefield as a pure planeswalker.

This is directly analogous to the scenario in [Animate Dead ruling #4], where the returned creature can't legally be enchanted by Animate Dead for some reason (there it's protection from black; here it's that the object is no longer a creature at all): Animate Dead is put into your graveyard as a state-based action, which causes its "When this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it" delayed trigger to fire. When that trigger resolves, Grist, the Hunger Tide is still on the battlefield, so you, as its controller, must sacrifice it [Animate Dead ruling #4].

Net effect: Grist, the Hunger Tide comes onto the battlefield as a planeswalker with its printed starting loyalty (3), Animate Dead immediately falls off and goes to your graveyard, and then Grist, the Hunger Tide is sacrificed once that leaves-the-battlefield trigger resolves. There is a brief window where Grist, the Hunger Tide is a legal planeswalker on the battlefield between these events, but it will not stick around — you won't get to keep it or use its loyalty abilities before it's sacrificed, since all of this happens through triggered abilities and state-based actions without you getting to act on it in between in any way that saves it.

Assumption: I'm assuming no other effect (like an alternate way to make Grist a creature again, or protection, or an effect changing what Animate Dead enchants) is in play; any such effect could change this outcome.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

cited_text.702.128a: Embalm Embalm is an activated ability that functions while the card with embalm is in a graveyard. “Embalm [cost]” means “[Cost], Exile this card from your graveyard: Create a token that’s a copy of this card, except it’s white, it has no mana cost, and it’s a Zombie in addition to its other types. Activate only as a sorcery.”
